guides.title: Your first week of yoga
guides.subtitle: A welcoming place to begin
guides.intro: Your first week is a chance to get acquainted, not to prove anything. Expect unfamiliar words, moments of wobbling, and plenty of choices. A short practice can be a complete practice.

sections.heading: 1 · Make a little space
sections.body: Choose a place where you can stretch your arms without meeting furniture. A mat can offer grip, though a steady chair also makes a useful starting point. Keep a blanket within reach and wear clothing that lets you move comfortably. Before pressing play, notice how you feel today. You do not need to arrive relaxed or flexible. You only need permission to begin at your own pace.

sections.heading: 2 · Learn a few familiar shapes
sections.body: During your first sessions, you may meet Mountain, a gentle fold, and a resting position. Treat their names as helpful labels rather than tests to pass. Watch a demonstration before trying something unfamiliar, then move slowly enough to notice your footing and breathing. If following every transition feels busy, pause the recording. Repeating one simple shape can teach you more than hurrying through a whole sequence.

sections.heading: 3 · Expect choices, not perfection
sections.body: Your teacher may offer bent knees, a chair, or a shorter hold. Those choices are part of yoga, not a separate practice for people who cannot do it properly. Explore a comfortable range and leave room for ordinary breathing. Sharp sensations, numbness, or dizziness are reasons to stop, rather than invitations to persevere. If you have an injury or a health concern, ask a qualified professional about appropriate movement.

sections.heading: 4 · Finish with a moment of noticing
sections.body: At the end, sit or lie in a position you can leave easily. Notice the contact beneath you and let your breathing be ordinary. You might feel settled, restless, or simply ready for breakfast. None of those responses measures the quality of your practice. For your first week, choose a few short sessions and leave space between them when you want it. Familiarity grows through kind repetition.

takeaways: Begin with a few familiar movements.
Use support whenever it helps.
Notice your experience without grading it.

guides.title: Breath is the practice
guides.subtitle: Explore ujjayi without forcing the sound
guides.intro: Breathing gives movement a rhythm, but it does not need to become another task to master. Begin with your ordinary breath, then explore a quieter pace and an optional introduction to ujjayi.

sections.heading: 1 · Listen before changing anything
sections.body: Settle into a comfortable seat or stand with support nearby. Notice where breathing moves your body without trying to make it deeper. Your ribs may widen, your belly may move, or the sensations may be quite subtle. Let several breaths pass this way. This simple observation is already practice. If paying close attention to breathing feels uncomfortable, turn your attention toward the contact of your feet instead.

sections.heading: 2 · Meet the sound of ujjayi
sections.body: Ujjayi is often taught with a gentle narrowing at the throat that gives the breath a soft, oceanlike sound. Try a quiet sigh through an open mouth, as though fogging a mirror. Then, if comfortable, close your mouth and keep only a trace of that quality while breathing through your nose. The sound should be subtle, not scraped or pushed. Return to ordinary breathing whenever your throat feels strained.

sections.heading: 3 · Let movement follow the breath
sections.body: Try lifting your arms on an easy inhale and lowering them on an easy exhale. Keep the movement small enough that you do not need to gulp air or speed through the end. One breath does not have to carry every transition. Take an extra breath while standing, seated, or resting whenever you need it. Matching movement and breath is an exploration of attention, not a rule you must obey.

sections.heading: 4 · Keep ease as your reference
sections.body: You can practice yoga without ujjayi, and you do not need to breathe through your nose when that feels difficult. Choose an ordinary, unforced rhythm instead. Stop the exercise if you notice dizziness, breathlessness, or agitation, and allow breathing to settle naturally. Avoid trying to make the breath louder as effort increases. A quieter movement, a shorter hold, or a pause may be the more useful next step.

takeaways: Start by observing your natural breath.
Keep ujjayi soft and optional.
Take extra breaths whenever you need them.

guides.title: Sun Salutation A, pose by pose
guides.subtitle: A breath-linked beginner variation
guides.intro: Sun Salutation A has several teaching variations. This introduction uses a gentle Cobra pathway rather than requiring Chaturanga or Upward Dog. Learn the shapes separately, then connect them with room for extra breaths.

sections.heading: 1 · Rise from Mountain
sections.body: Begin in Mountain with your feet together or comfortably apart and your arms resting by your sides. Feel the floor through both feet. Inhale into Upward Salute, lifting your arms only as far as your shoulders welcome. Exhale into Forward Fold, bending your knees generously and hinging at your hips. Your hands can land on your shins, sturdy supports, or the floor. Reaching the ground is not the goal.

sections.heading: 2 · Lengthen and step back
sections.body: Inhale into Halfway Lift, bringing your hands to your shins or supports and lengthening your spine forward. Keep your neck following the line of your back. Exhale and place your hands on the floor, bending your knees as much as needed. Step back into Plank, with shoulders above wrists, or lower your knees immediately. Pause for another breath if you need time to arrange your hands and find steady support.

sections.heading: 3 · Choose your lowering pathway
sections.body: From Plank, lower your knees and then your torso toward the floor on an exhale. For a Knees-Chest-Chin variation, keep knees down, bend elbows close, and lower chest and chin only if your neck welcomes it; otherwise lower belly down. Inhale into a small Cobra with elbows bent and pelvis grounded. Upward Dog is an alternative for experienced practitioners, with thighs lifted and weight through hands and tops of feet.

sections.heading: 4 · Return with room to breathe
sections.body: Exhale toward Downward Dog, passing through hands and knees if that feels more manageable. Keep your knees bent and let your heels stay lifted. Take several ordinary breaths, or rest on hands and knees instead. Look forward, then step toward your hands in as many small steps as needed. Inhale to Halfway Lift, exhale to Fold, inhale to rise through Upward Salute, and exhale your arms back into Mountain.

takeaways: Learn each shape before linking the sequence.
Choose the lowering variation that suits you.
Add breaths rather than rushing transitions.

guides.title: Alignment basics: feet, knees, spine
guides.subtitle: Useful landmarks, not a perfect silhouette
guides.intro: Alignment is a conversation between your body, the ground, and the movement you are exploring. These simple landmarks can help you make thoughtful adjustments without chasing a single correct-looking shape.

sections.heading: 1 · Find your foundation
sections.body: Stand with your feet a comfortable distance apart. Notice the base of each big toe, the base of each little toe, and the heel meeting the ground. Let your toes rest rather than gripping for control. Gently shift your weight forward and back, then settle somewhere centered. Your feet do not need to look identical. Explore the stance that allows you to stand and breathe without unnecessary effort.

sections.heading: 2 · Give your knees some room
sections.body: As you bend into a standing pose, let each knee travel broadly in the direction of its middle toes. This is a useful reference, not a demand to force your legs into parallel lines. Adjust the distance between your feet or make the bend smaller if the position feels awkward. Avoid pressing a straight knee backward to create a finished appearance. Keep enough freedom to change direction or step out.

sections.heading: 3 · Let your spine respond
sections.body: Imagine your spine lengthening without pulling your ribs upward or holding your belly rigid. Your back has natural curves, so length does not mean flattening everything into a straight line. In a forward fold, bend your knees and tip from your hips before reaching farther. In a twist, begin with a comfortable upright position and turn modestly. Let your head follow rather than leading with a forceful pull.

sections.heading: 4 · Use feedback, not a photograph
sections.body: A photograph shows an outline, but it cannot tell you how a pose feels from inside. Check whether you can breathe freely, release your jaw, and leave the position with control. A wall, chair, or teacher can give useful feedback when you are unsure. If something feels sharp, pinching, or numb, come out. Alignment is useful when it helps you pay attention, not when it becomes another reason to judge yourself.

takeaways: Build your pose from the ground upward.
Let knees follow the direction of your toes.
Prioritize breathing and choice over appearance.

guides.title: Yin and restorative
guides.subtitle: Two ways to explore a slower practice
guides.intro: Yin and restorative yoga both make room for stillness, but they are not interchangeable. Understanding the difference can help you choose the kind of quiet practice that suits your day.

sections.heading: 1 · Understand the difference
sections.body: Yin yoga usually explores sustained, mostly floor-based shapes with a modest stretch sensation. Restorative yoga uses generous support so that holding the shape asks for very little muscular effort. A yin position may feel quietly active through sensation, while a restorative position aims to feel restful from the start. Neither style asks you to endure discomfort. You can choose a shorter stay, a different position, or another kind of practice.

sections.heading: 2 · Set up before settling
sections.body: Gather a cushion, a blanket, and any firm supports you have available. For a simple restorative rest, lie on your back with a cushion beneath your knees and a folded blanket under your head if helpful. Arrange things so your neck feels comfortable and your breathing is easy. Take time to adjust before becoming still. More support is useful when it makes the position easier to inhabit, not more elaborate.

sections.heading: 3 · Stay curious about sensation
sections.body: In yin, begin with a small range and an initial stay of a few comfortable breaths rather than copying a long hold. Sensation should leave room for ease and ordinary breathing. Do not use your body weight to force a joint farther, and leave any position that brings sharpness, tingling, or numbness. If you are very flexible or have joint concerns, seek individualized guidance before exploring sustained end-range positions.

sections.heading: 4 · Leave slowly and freely
sections.body: When you are ready to move, let your first movement be small. Bend a knee, return your hands to the floor, or roll to your side before sitting up. Pause in a neutral position and notice what you want next. Quiet practice can bring restlessness as well as ease; you have not done it wrong if you prefer to move. Stillness is an invitation you can accept, shorten, or decline.

takeaways: Yin explores sensation; restorative emphasizes support.
Start with shorter stays and modest ranges.
Change position whenever your body asks.

guides.title: Making yoga work for your body
guides.subtitle: Everyday props and practical modifications
guides.intro: Your home already holds useful practice tools. A chair, wall, cushion, blanket, and a few sturdy books can change the distance, effort, and balance a pose asks of you.

sections.heading: 1 · Bring the floor closer
sections.body: In a standing fold, rest your hands on the seat of a sturdy chair instead of reaching for the floor. Place the chair against a wall so it cannot slide away, and avoid wheeled or folding chairs. Bend your knees and keep the fold small. You can also practice seated, leaning forward with hands on thighs. The useful version is the one that lets you move and return with control.

sections.heading: 2 · Let the wall offer feedback
sections.body: Stand beside a wall for balance practice and place a hand against it before lifting a foot. In a simple Tree variation, keep your lifted toes on the floor with the heel resting near the opposite ankle. You can stay there for the whole practice. A wall also offers a place for an upright standing push away, with palms supported and feet stepped back only as far as feels comfortable.

sections.heading: 3 · Choose household props carefully
sections.body: A folded blanket can cushion your knees, and a firm cushion can raise your seat so sitting feels less cramped. Thick books can bring a surface closer for light hand support, but choose firm, nonslippery books of equal height. Keep stacks low and stable. Books are not designed as exercise equipment, so do not balance on them or use them for substantial weight bearing. Choose a chair or wall instead.

sections.heading: 4 · Adapt the task, not your worth
sections.body: A modification changes what a pose asks of you. It does not lower the value of your practice. Try widening your stance, shortening a hold, skipping a transition, or remaining seated while the teacher stands. If a cue does not make sense in your body, pause and explore a smaller version. For ongoing discomfort or specific movement restrictions, seek individualized guidance rather than trying to solve everything with a prop.

takeaways: Use a stable chair or wall for support.
Keep improvised props low and secure.
Change the pose to meet your needs.

guides.title: Pranayama for everyday calm
guides.subtitle: Four gentle ways to explore the breath
guides.intro: Pranayama is the yogic practice of working with the breath. These introductions invite attention rather than big results. Practice seated and unhurried, never while driving, swimming, or doing anything that needs your full attention.

sections.heading: 1 · Begin with belly breathing
sections.body: Rest a hand lightly over your belly while sitting comfortably or lying with your knees supported. Let the inhale bring whatever movement arrives naturally beneath your hand, then allow the exhale to leave without pressing. You do not need to push your belly outward or fill your lungs completely. Try a few ordinary breaths. If the exercise creates air hunger or unease, stop shaping the breath and notice your surroundings instead.

sections.heading: 2 · Explore a smaller box
sections.body: Box breathing uses four equal phases: inhale, pause, exhale, pause. Start by imagining a small box with a comfortable count of two along each side, and try only a few cycles. Pauses are optional; simply inhale and exhale evenly if holding feels unpleasant. Avoid breath retention during pregnancy or with cardiovascular or respiratory conditions unless your clinician advises otherwise. Dizziness or breathlessness means stop and return to natural breathing.

sections.heading: 3 · Alternate without holding
sections.body: For a simple alternate nostril practice, use a clean hand and gentle touch. Close the right nostril, inhale through the left, switch, and exhale through the right. Inhale through the right, switch, and exhale through the left to complete one round. Keep the breath light and omit holds. If your nose is blocked, do not pull air through resistance. You can simply imagine alternating sides while breathing naturally instead.

sections.heading: 4 · Try a quiet bee breath
sections.body: For bee breath, or bhramari, inhale gently and make a soft humming sound as you exhale through your nose with lips together. Keep your hands resting and leave your ears uncovered for this introduction. Try two or three rounds, without stretching the exhale beyond comfort. Stop if you feel pressure, dizziness, or agitation. If you have a relevant health condition or breathing practice triggers panic, ask a qualified professional for guidance.

takeaways: Keep every breathing exercise comfortable and optional.
Skip holds when they are unsuitable.
Stop for dizziness, breathlessness, or distress.

guides.title: Building a habit that lasts
guides.subtitle: Make room for ten minutes a day
guides.intro: Ten minutes can hold a meaningful practice, but it need not become a daily demand. Build a routine around a reliable cue, a manageable plan, and the freedom to begin again.

sections.heading: 1 · Choose a cue you already have
sections.body: Look for a moment that already belongs to your day, such as finishing breakfast or closing your work laptop. Place a short practice beside that moment instead of waiting for a perfect opening. Choose somewhere you can begin without rearranging the whole room. A visible blanket or a chair placed thoughtfully can serve as a reminder. Let the cue say that practice is available, not that you have fallen behind.

sections.heading: 2 · Give ten minutes a simple shape
sections.body: Begin with a minute of noticing your feet and your natural breath. Spend the next few minutes on familiar movements, perhaps a standing reach, a supported fold, and gentle chair Cat and Cow. Leave time for a comfortable seated or lying rest. You do not need a new sequence every day. Familiarity can make starting easier because you already know the first movement and can adjust it as you go.

sections.heading: 3 · Keep a smaller version ready
sections.body: Some days ten minutes will fit, and some days it will not. Decide in advance what your smaller practice looks like. It might be three unhurried reaches or a minute sitting with your feet on the floor. This is not a trick for forcing yourself to do more afterward. Let the small version count on its own. You are keeping a relationship with practice, not meeting a quota at any cost.

sections.heading: 4 · Return without catching up
sections.body: A missed day does not require a longer session tomorrow. Return to your usual cue and choose what fits the body and attention you have now. Occasionally ask whether your routine still serves you. A different time, a seated option, or planned days off may make it more sustainable. You can notice consistency without turning it into a score. The useful habit is learning how to return with kindness.

takeaways: Attach practice to an existing daily cue.
Keep a smaller version ready for busy days.
Begin again without trying to catch up.

guides.title: The eight limbs of yoga
guides.subtitle: Patanjali's map, in plain words
guides.intro: Around two thousand years ago, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali gathered yoga into short, dense lines. One of them describes yoga as eight limbs, ashtanga. Postures are only one of the eight, which is why yoga has always been about more than flexibility.

sections.heading: 1 · Yama and niyama: how we live
sections.body: The first two limbs are about conduct. The yamas look outward: non-harming (ahimsa), truthfulness (satya), not taking what is not given (asteya), wise use of energy (brahmacharya) and non-grasping (aparigraha). The niyamas look inward: cleanliness (saucha), contentment (santosha), steady effort (tapas), self-study (svadhyaya) and surrender to something larger than yourself (ishvara pranidhana). On the mat, ahimsa can be as simple as choosing a gentler version of a pose today.

sections.heading: 2 · Asana and pranayama: body and breath
sections.body: The Sutras say very little about postures. The key line, sthira sukham asanam, asks that a posture be steady and easy at the same time. That is still a useful test: if you are straining or holding your breath, back off until both are present. Pranayama, the fourth limb, means extending or guiding the breath. Techniques such as Ujjayi and alternate-nostril breathing grew from this idea. Gentle, unforced breathing always comes first.

sections.heading: 3 · Pratyahara and dharana: turning inward
sections.body: Pratyahara means drawing the senses inward, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. It is the moment in practice when outside sounds stop pulling at you and attention rests inside. Dharana is concentration: holding attention on one point, such as the breath, a sound, or a candle flame. In a balance pose like Tree, you practise both at once. The mind wanders constantly; the skill is in noticing and returning.

sections.heading: 4 · Dhyana and samadhi: meditation and absorption
sections.body: When concentration becomes continuous and effortless, the Sutras call it dhyana, meditation. Samadhi, the last limb, describes complete absorption, where the sense of a separate observer quietens. You do not need to chase these states. They are described as the natural result of the earlier limbs practised patiently over time. A few minutes of quiet sitting after your practice is a real step on the same path.

takeaways: Postures are one limb of eight.
A pose should be steady and easy at once.
Concentration grows by noticing and returning.

guides.title: The seven chakras, simply
guides.subtitle: An ancient map for attention
guides.intro: Chakra means wheel. In tantric and later Hatha yoga texts, the chakras are described as centres along the spine, each with its own element, seed sound and image. They are best understood as a traditional map for directing attention, rather than as physical organs or a medical system.

sections.heading: 1 · Root, sacral and navel
sections.body: Muladhara, the root, sits at the base of the spine and is linked with earth and the seed sound Lam. Practice for it feels grounded: standing poses, squats, slow breathing. Svadhisthana, below the navel, is linked with water and Vam, and suits fluid hip work. Manipura, the jewel city at the navel, is linked with fire and Ram. Core strength, twists and warming flows are traditional companions to it.

sections.heading: 2 · Heart and throat
sections.body: Anahata, at the centre of the chest, is linked with air and the seed sound Yam. Its name means unstruck, a sound that arises without being made. Gentle backbends and kindness practices such as metta suit it well. Vishuddha, at the throat, is linked with space and Ham. Easing the neck and jaw, Fish Pose and humming breath are classic ways to bring attention there.

sections.heading: 3 · Brow and crown
sections.body: Ajna sits between the eyebrows and is linked with the sound Om. Many traditions use this point for concentration, so balance poses and steady-gaze practices fit naturally. Sahasrara, at the crown of the head, is pictured as a lotus of a thousand petals and described as beyond the elements. Here, practice becomes quiet sitting and rest in open awareness.

sections.heading: 4 · About the colours
sections.body: The rainbow colours often shown today, red at the root through to violet at the crown, are a modern addition that many people find helpful for visualisation. Older texts describe different colours, numbers of petals and deities for each centre. Whichever images you use, the practical value is the same: a structured way to move attention through the body, from stability to stillness.

takeaways: Chakras are a traditional map for attention.
Each centre has an element and a seed sound.
Practice moves from grounding to stillness.

guides.title: Hatha: the sun and the moon
guides.subtitle: Why yoga balances effort and ease
guides.intro: Hatha yoga is often explained as ha, the sun, and tha, the moon. Classical texts such as the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, written in the fifteenth century, describe practices that balance these two qualities: warming and cooling, effort and ease.

sections.heading: 1 · Surya: the warming side
sections.body: Solar practice is active and heating. Surya Namaskar, the Sun Salutation, links each movement with one breath and warms the whole body in a few minutes. Standing poses, strong holds and brisk breathing practices such as an optional Kapalabhati belong here. Solar days suit cool mornings or times when you feel heavy and slow.

sections.heading: 2 · Chandra: the cooling side
sections.body: Lunar practice is slower and calming. Chandra Namaskar, the Moon Salutation, moves side to side through crescent side bends, Goddess, Triangle, Pyramid, lunges and a deep squat. It favours the hips and the side body and pairs well with long exhalations and alternate-nostril breathing. Lunar days suit evenings or times when you feel overheated or restless.

sections.heading: 3 · Balancing the two
sections.body: Most good classes contain both: a warming middle and a cooling end. You can also choose the side you need. If you feel sluggish, add a few rounds of Sun Salutation. If you feel wired, try Moon Salutation and a slow breath. Even inside a single pose, look for both qualities: firm legs and a soft face, an active core and an easy breath.

sections.heading: 4 · A note on breath
sections.body: Traditional texts link the right nostril with the sun and the left with the moon. Moon breath, inhaling through the left nostril, is used to quieten; alternate-nostril breathing aims for balance. Keep every breathing practice gentle, skip holds and fast breathing during pregnancy or if you have a health concern, and return to natural breathing whenever you feel light-headed.

takeaways: Sun practice warms; moon practice cools.
Good practice holds effort and ease together.
Choose the side you need today.

guides.title: Ayurveda and the three doshas
guides.subtitle: Match your practice to how you feel
guides.intro: Ayurveda is the traditional system of wellbeing from India, often called yoga's sister science. It describes three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, as combinations of the elements that shape our moods and energy. Used in yoga, they offer a practical way to choose what kind of practice you need today. They are not a diagnosis or a treatment.

sections.heading: 1 · Vata: air and space
sections.body: Vata is light, quick and changeable, like the wind. When it feels high you might notice a busy mind, restlessness or scattered energy. Practice that balances it is slow, warm and grounding: standing poses with the feet firmly planted, long holds, forward folds, and a calm breath with a longer exhale. Keep transitions smooth and finish with a generous rest.

sections.heading: 2 · Pitta: fire and water
sections.body: Pitta is hot, sharp and driven. When it runs high you might feel impatient, competitive or overheated. Cooling, non-competitive practice helps: Moon Salutations, gentle backbends, wide seated folds, twists and humming or cooling breath. Practise at around seventy per cent of your effort, and let go of measuring yourself against yesterday.

sections.heading: 3 · Kapha: earth and water
sections.body: Kapha is steady, soft and stable, like the earth. When it feels heavy you might notice sluggishness or low motivation. Energising practice balances it: brisk Sun Salutations, standing strength, balances, chest openers and, if it suits you, a gentle energising breath. Start a little faster than feels natural; energy often follows movement.

sections.heading: 4 · Using the doshas wisely
sections.body: Everyone contains all three qualities, and how you feel changes with the season, the time of day and your life. Rather than labelling yourself, ask a simple question before practice: do I need grounding, cooling or energising today? Then choose accordingly. For any health concern, speak to a qualified healthcare professional rather than relying on dosha-based advice.

takeaways: Vata needs grounding, pitta cooling, kapha energy.
Ask what you need today, not what you are.
The doshas guide practice, not treatment.

tips.title: Let your knees bend
tips.body: In a standing fold, bend your knees enough to let your torso move comfortably toward your thighs.

tips.title: Start with ordinary breath
tips.body: Before changing your breathing, notice a few natural cycles. There is nothing you need to achieve.

tips.title: Put support within reach
tips.body: Set a chair or folded blanket beside your mat before practice so you can use it without interrupting your flow.

tips.title: Keep Tree close to the ground
tips.body: Try Tree with your lifted toes touching the floor. A hand on the wall can offer another point of support.

tips.title: Take another breath
tips.body: If a transition feels rushed, pause in a stable position and take an extra breath before moving on.

tips.title: Let your heels hover
tips.body: Your heels do not have to touch the floor in Downward Dog. Bend your knees and leave room for your spine.

tips.title: Choose a smaller Cobra
tips.body: Lift only as far as your back welcomes. Keep elbows bent rather than pushing toward straight arms.

tips.title: Rest before you need to
tips.body: You can step out of a sequence before feeling exhausted. Resting is a choice, not a reward.

tips.title: Make your seat comfortable
tips.body: Sit on a folded blanket if it helps you find an easy upright position. A chair is an equally useful option.

tips.title: Give your jaw a break
tips.body: Notice whether you are clenching your teeth in a pose. Let your jaw soften while your breathing stays ordinary.

tips.title: Look somewhere steady
tips.body: For balance, choose a still point at eye level or slightly lower. Keep support close enough to reach.

tips.title: Try the quiet version
tips.body: Ujjayi does not need to be loud. If it feels strained, return to your natural breath.

tips.title: Keep your water nearby
tips.body: Have water available and pause for a sip when you want one. You do not need to follow the recording without breaks.

tips.title: Let the chair stay still
tips.body: Use a sturdy chair without wheels and place it against a wall before leaning your hands onto it.

tips.title: Mark a gentle beginning
tips.body: Choose one word, such as steady or curious, before practice. Let it guide your attention rather than set a goal.

tips.title: Leave a little room
tips.body: Stop short of your deepest stretch and notice whether a smaller range gives you more freedom to breathe.

tips.title: Pause after practice
tips.body: Before reaching for your phone, take a moment to notice the floor beneath you.

tips.title: Make tomorrow easier
tips.body: Leave a blanket or mat where you will see it at your chosen practice time.

tips.title: Shorten the session
tips.body: When time is tight, choose a few familiar movements instead of rushing through a longer sequence.

tips.title: Skip the comparison
tips.body: Your pose can look different from the teacher’s. Use their cues as invitations to explore, not a silhouette to copy.

tips.title: Move out with care
tips.body: Come out of a held pose gradually, then pause before choosing your next movement.

tips.title: Let your hands spread
tips.body: In hands-and-knees positions, spread your fingers comfortably. Change position if your wrists feel uncomfortable.

tips.title: Start from your chair
tips.body: A seated reach and gentle spinal movement can be your whole practice today.

tips.title: Try a music-free minute
tips.body: Notice the sounds already around you while you practice one familiar movement.

tips.title: Morning is optional
tips.body: Choose the time you can return to, whether that is after breakfast or before bed.

tips.title: Keep breath holds optional
tips.body: If a breathing exercise includes pauses, skip them whenever they feel uncomfortable or are not appropriate for you.

tips.title: Notice sharp sensations
tips.body: Stop a movement that brings sharpness, tingling, or numbness. Do not push through to finish a pose.

tips.title: Let rest be ordinary
tips.body: You do not have to feel peaceful during rest. Notice what is present without trying to manufacture a mood.

tips.title: Count the small practice
tips.body: A minute of attentive movement is worth noticing. You can finish there without adding more.

tips.title: Finish with appreciation
tips.body: Name one thoughtful choice you made today, such as taking a break or using support.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: Asanova is a guided yoga, breathwork and meditation app. This policy explains what happens to your information when you use it. The short version: your answers, body details and practice history stay on your phone, the app contains no advertising or tracking tools, and purchases are handled by Apple or Google.

sections.h: Information that stays on your device
p: Your onboarding answers (such as age range, goals, body measurements, activity level, flexibility and balance, and any areas you want to protect), your plan, practice history, favourites, reminders and settings are stored only on your phone. Asanova has no accounts and does not upload this information.
You can erase it at any time in Profile → Reset all data, or by uninstalling the app.

When you use Tell us what you need, we store your message, optional reply email, submission time, app version and platform in a private inbox hosted by Lovable Cloud. Other app users cannot read these messages. No onboarding answers, practice history, purchase identifier or advertising identifier is attached. Please do not include health or payment details.

We use these messages to respond to requests and improve the app, not for advertising. Our hosting provider also processes technical connection information to deliver the request. To request access or deletion, email pranacodes@gmail.com and identify your message.
We retain messages only as long as needed to handle the request and related follow-up. Resetting the app does not delete a message you have already sent.
Payments are processed by the Apple App Store or Google Play under their own terms. We never see your card or payment details. Your Asanova Plus status is kept on your phone.
Asanova contains no advertising SDKs, analytics trackers or ad-measurement tools. We do not collect your advertising identifier and we do not share your activity with advertisers or data brokers.
Practice reminders are scheduled locally on your phone; no push service or notification token is used. Coaching voice, music and films are bundled with the app and play offline.

Because your practice data never leaves your phone, you control it directly. For a message you sent us, you can ask us to access or delete it by emailing us. You may also complain to your local data protection authority.

On-device data stays until you reset it or uninstall the app. Purchase records are kept by Apple or Google as required for tax and accounting. Messages you send travel over encrypted connections and may be processed outside your country under our provider's safeguards.
Asanova is made for adults. It is not directed to children under 16, and we do not knowingly collect information from them.
If we change what is collected or shared, we will update this policy and tell you in the app.
Questions or requests: pranacodes@gmail.com.
